opus-5.5.text:
I think Freeman Dyson's distinction is a really useful lens. In his essay, he said some scientists are birds: they fly high in the air and survey broad vistas, looking for unifying ideas that connect problems across different fields. Others are frogs: they live in the mud, look at the details of one particular thing, and solve problems one at a time. Dyson himself said he was a frog, and he argued that science needs both kinds.

For Max, my impression from working with him as his student is that he is very much a bird, but a bird who is not afraid to land. He has this habit of zooming out and asking, "What's the big picture here? What's the simplest principle that could explain all of these things?" You can see it in his career. He started in cosmology, precision measurements of the cosmic microwave background, then went to the foundations of quantum mechanics, then to the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis, which is about as bird-like as an idea can get. And then he moved into AI and AI safety. To an outsider these look like totally different fields. To Max, they're connected by one question: how do we understand the universe, and how do we understand the minds that understand the universe?

But what I appreciate most is that he doesn't stay up in the clouds. When we work on a concrete project, say interpretability of neural networks or what became KAN, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, he really cares about getting a clean, minimal example working. He often says something like, "Let's find the simplest toy model where this phenomenon shows up." That's very physicist-like. In physics you study the hydrogen atom before complicated molecules. So he flies high to choose the direction, then dives down to find the cleanest piece of ground to stand on.

For me personally, I'd say I'm somewhere in between, maybe a frog who keeps looking up at the sky. I enjoy getting my hands dirty with experiments, training many small networks, watching the loss curves, but I always ask what the general lesson is. Being around Max pushed me toward the bird side. He'd look at a result I was excited about and ask, "Okay, but why should anyone outside this subfield care?" That question is annoying at first, but it's very healthy.

I'd also add that AI right now especially needs birds. The field is dominated by frogs, in a good sense: lots of people pushing benchmarks, tweaking architectures, scaling things up. That's produced amazing progress. But we lack a unifying understanding of why these systems work. It's a bit like the era before thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, when we had steam engines but no theory of heat. People like Max, who bring a physicist's bird's-eye view, can help us move from alchemy toward something more like a science of intelligence. I think that's the deeper reason he moved into AI: he sees it as the next frontier where a bird's perspective can make a real difference.

fable-5.1.text:
Dyson's picture is that birds fly high and see the whole landscape, connecting distant fields, while frogs live in the mud and love the details of one particular problem. Max is very clearly a bird. When I first joined his group, what struck me was that he almost never starts from a specific technical problem. He starts from a very big question, like "what is intelligence, really?" or "can we make AI understandable to humans?", and then works downward to find a concrete place where a physicist could actually do something.

That's the physicist's instinct in him. He is always looking for the simple, unifying principle underneath a messy phenomenon, the way physicists look for a conservation law. In our work on AI for physics and physics for AI, he keeps asking whether the thing we found in a neural network is just a curiosity, or whether it reflects some deeper structure. He is much less interested in beating a benchmark by a few percent than in whether a result changes how we think.

But I would add that being a bird doesn't mean being vague. Max is very good at compressing a big idea into a sharp, testable question, and then handing it to a frog, which is often a student like me. That's really how the collaboration works. I enjoy sitting in the mud with the details of a specific network or a specific symbolic regression problem, and he keeps pulling me back up to ask what it means. I think the best science usually needs both, and the reason the lab is productive is that the two perspectives keep correcting each other.

astra-6.text:
I think Dyson’s distinction is useful here: birds look at the landscape from above and try to see how everything connects, while frogs stay close to the ground and work through particular problems in detail. Max strikes me as very much a bird. He likes to ask big questions, examine the assumptions behind them, and look for a framework that connects things that initially seem unrelated.

But being a bird isn’t simply about asking ambitious questions. The challenge is finding a place where a broad idea becomes something precise that you can actually investigate. That’s how I would understand his way of thinking: start with the big picture, then look for a concrete question that gives you a foothold.

And I don’t think the distinction is a ranking. You need both perspectives. Without the bird, you can lose sight of why a problem matters; without the frog, you can mistake an appealing picture for an explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Max is very much a bird in Dyson’s sense. A frog looks closely at a particular problem and discovers things by working through the details. A bird looks from above and asks how different problems fit into a larger picture.

Max often starts with a very broad question: What is intelligence? What is the relationship between mathematics and the physical world? Then he tries to find a simple framework that makes the question precise. That willingness to step back and question the framing is, to me, the bird part of his thinking.

But the distinction isn’t absolute. You need to come back down and do the frog work—calculations, experiments, checking whether your beautiful idea actually works. What I find valuable is the movement between those perspectives: let the big question guide the technical work, and let the technical work change your big picture.
